samples_judged.question_text: A ball has a surface that bends smoothly in every direction. What kind of surface does a ball have?
A ball has a surface that bends smoothly in every direction. What kind of surface does a ball have?

samples_judged.correct_answer: Because it never bends or changes direction.

samples_judged.question_text: The edge of a desk never bends or changes direction. Which best describes it?

samples_judged.correct_answer: A ball has a curved surface, but a box has flat surfaces.

verdicts.reasoning: Each item gives a described object or property and asks the student to select the correct category label ('Which best describes it?' / 'What kind of surface...'), which is identification.

Seed 42 asks 'Why is the edge of a ruler called a straight line?' and 103/118 ask why a ball rolls and a box does not; the keys are reasons, not labels. Caveat recorded by the Attester: every explanation is recognition among four supplied options - no item asks the student to produce an explanation in their own words.

verdicts.reasoning: PROVIDED thinly. Seeds 103/118 only - their key sets two categories against each other; every other item requires one label in isolation, and 103/118 are the same stem twice. The Attester noted no item ever contrasts a straight line against a curved line, though the competency names that pair first.
Seeds 42 and 57 key 'straight line' ('never bends or changes direction'); seed 64 uses 'straight ruler' in the stem.
PROVIDED once. Seed 78 (winding river) is the only item in all 10 where 'curved line' is the answer; it appears as a distractor in seven others.
Seed 64 keys 'flat surface'; 103/118 key an answer naming 'flat surfaces'. The Attester flagged seed 64 as itself defective, and it is the only item targeting flat alone.
Over-represented rather than absent: seeds 11/23/91/127 key 'curved surface' outright and 103/118 name it in the key.
Seeds 64/91/127 use 'solid figure'; ball, box and desk are the objects. The term '3-dimensional' never appears in student text, which the Attester judged appropriate for Grade 2 rather than a gap.

incidental_findings.finding: Answer key is defensibly wrong and the discriminator is mathematically false. 'Which best describes the side of a solid figure that you could trace with a straight ruler?' keys 'flat surface', but 'straight line' is in the option set and better fits what the stem literally describes (a ruler traces a line, not a surface). Traceability with a straightedge does not identify a flat surface: the lateral surface of a cylinder or cone contains straight lines. 'side' is also ambiguous between face and edge - the very distinction the item tests.

incidental_findings.finding: Answer-in-stem: the defining property is stated in the stem and the student need only match it to a label. Seeds 91/127 additionally give it away with 'like a ball'. Seed 42 uses the straight-line phrase as the key while seed 57 uses the identical phrase as the stem, so the set is answerable by keyword match.
Distractor 'A ball is always heavier than a box' tests neither lines nor surfaces and does not probe the misconception space.

Lopsided by keyed target: curved surface 6 of 10; straight line 2; curved line exactly 1 (seed 78); flat surface exactly 1 (seed 64), and that one is the defective item - so a student may meet no sound flat-surface item at all. 10 samples contain 7 distinct items (11=23, 91=127, 103=118). 'difference between' is exercised only on the surface pair, never straight-vs-curved line. Objects are limited to ball, box and desk; no named solid (cube, sphere, cylinder, cone), so the coexistence case (a cylinder having both surface kinds) is never touched.
Vocabulary judged in range for Grade 2 throughout. 'winding' is the hardest word but is glossed in the same sentence ('bends smoothly and changes direction'), so it is not a gate.
